newsitem.title: UK: "Bad" news for emerging debt markets brings relief.
newsitem.headline: "Bad" news for emerging debt markets brings relief.

text.p: A plunge in emerging debt prices, triggered by fears of higher U.S. interest rates, is probably good for the market and far from marks the end of the road for one of the world's fastest rising assets, fund managers and analysts said on Tuesday.

"I'm glad it's selling off. Otherwise the market keeps going up and it becomes unsustainable...Though we recognise we're losing money for the moment, in the long-run it's more healthy," said Michael Mabbutt, emerging market fixed income fund manager at LGT Assett Management.
"You shake out the recent joiners who thought this was a one-way bet and who can be dangerous for a market," he added.
Emerging debt prices rose by about a third on average last year and showed no signs of stopping in the first two months of 1997.
Then U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan last week jolted investors by, what many took to be, implying that U.S. interest rates would rise soon.
His comments slashed four percent off the market in three days and spreads over U.S. Treasuries for Brady bonds ballooned 75 basis points to an average 470 by Monday's close of trading.
Some traders said Greenspan's comments were as much as anything an excuse to sell, and cash in some profits.

"It doesn't mean the emerging debt market is dead until the Fed eases again. There is enough interest in the market for interest to continue to pick up," said James Edwards, a fund manager at Foreign & Colonial.
And by Tuesday, there were already signs of a recovery in Brady bond prices.
But Simon Treacher, portfolio manager at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, warned that the market would probably see more volatility until the Federal Reserve's meeting on March 25.

"But as soon as (U.S.) Treasuries calm down, there is pent-up demand for this market. There is no fundamental reason for the market to collapse," he added, noting many investors were looking at the market for the longer-term.
Analysts cautioned against comparing the latest jitters over U.S. interest rates to 1994 when their increase brought an unhappy end to the emerging market bull run.

"Emerging market debt now looks vulnerable because it is so high and spreads are so tight. However, we doubt whether we will see a major correction in the near future," ABN-AMRO economist Ian Campbell said.
This time round, U.S. monetary policy has already been tight for three years and any more moves will be fine-tuning rather than a fundamental change.
Also, the main emerging markets are much less vulnerable to a tightening in international liqudity, Campbell said.
The Brady bond market has changed since those days to one that has become more liquid and with a much broader base of investor, who treats it now more like a standard bond market, analysts said.
Mabbutt said this has given the market more credibility and predicted it would become more stable.
"At 450 to 500 basis points (over U.S. Treasuries)it is still an attractive yield...If it gets to to 600, it's a big buy. That might happen under conditions of Fed tightening," he said.
